title: Motorbike Rental in Saigon: Everything You Need to Know
subtitle: (2026 Guide)
metaTitle: Motorbike Rental Saigon 2026 – Complete Guide | Red Lantern Bikes
metaDescription: Everything you need to know about renting a motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City: prices, which bike to choose, license rules, and where to pick up. Updated for 2026.
html:
Renting a motorbike in Ho Chi Minh City is one of the best decisions you can make as a traveler in Vietnam. There's no better way to feel the city's electric energy, discover hidden alleyways, and escape the tourist trail than on two wheels. But with so many rental shops, bike options, and confusing advice online, it's hard to know where to start.

This guide covers everything — prices, which bike to pick, license requirements, what's included, and how to stay safe. Updated for 2026.

How Much Does It Cost to Rent a Motorbike in Saigon?

Rental prices in Ho Chi Minh City range from around $9/day for a basic scooter to $42/day for a larger adventure bike. Here is what you can expect across the main categories:

• • Small scooter (Honda Wave 110cc): $7–$12/day — perfect for no pressure riding, easy for beginners

• • Mid-range manual (Honda XR150, Suzuki EN125): $10–$15/day — versatile, perfect for crossing Vietnam in 3weeks/1month

• • Large adventure bike (Honda CB150X, Kawasaki Versys X300): $42/day — best for serious long-distance touring

Weekly and monthly rates are significantly cheaper. If you plan to keep the bike for 7 days or more, always ask for a weekly rate — you can save 20–50% compared to the daily price.

Which Motorbike Should You Choose?

The right bike depends on your experience level, where you're going, and how long you're renting. Here's a simple breakdown:

For Beginners: Honda Wave Alpha 110cc

The Honda Wave is Vietnam's most popular bike for a reason. It's lightweight, semi- automatic, fuel-efficient, and incredibly easy to ride. If you've never ridden a motorbike before, this is where to start. It handles Saigon's chaotic traffic effortlessly and costs less than a coffee break per kilometer to run.

For cross country and offroading: Honda XR150, Honda CRF150, Yamaha WR155R

If you have some riding experience and want a bit more power for adventures and off the beaten path, the Honda XR150 and Yamaha WR155R are excellent choices. Both handle cross country comfortably while giving you enough engine to tackle coastal roads and rural routes with ease.

For Long-Distance Touring — Kawasaki Versys X300

Planning a one-way ride to Da Nang or Hanoi? The Kawasaki Versys X300 is the bike for you. With 300cc of power, a large top box included, and a comfortable upright riding position, it handles everything Vietnam can throw at you, mountain passes, long highway stretches, and narrow village roads.

Do I Need a License to Rent a Motorbike in Vietnam?

This is the most-asked question — and the answer is nuanced. Technically, you need a Vietnamese motorcycle license or an International Driving Permit (IDP) with a motorcycle category to legally ride in Vietnam. In practice, the enforcement varies significantly.

Here is what you actually need to know:

• • Bikes under 50cc (mopeds): no license required in Vietnam

• • Bikes 50–175cc (most rentals): Vietnamese license or IDP with motorbike category required

• • Bikes over 175cc: full Vietnamese motorcycle license required

• • Your home country driving license alone is NOT valid for riding in Vietnam

• • An IDP issued by your home country (based on the 1949 Geneva Convention) is accepted

At Red Lantern Bikes, we ask all customers about their license and can advise which bike category best suits their situation. We always recommend having the correct documentation — it protects you if you have an accident and need insurance to cover costs.

What's Included in the Rental?

A good rental shop should include more than just the bike. At Red Lantern Bikes, every rental includes:

• • Full-face helmet

• • Phone holder

• • Rack for bags or luggage

• • Bungee cords

• • Printed map of the best roads in Vietnam

• • Roadside assistance: call us if anything goes wrong, anywhere in Vietnam

Optional extras like insurance, premium helmets, side racks, top boxes, and hotel delivery are available at a small additional cost. We believe in zero hidden fees, the price you see is what you pay.

One-Way Rental: Rent in Saigon, Return Somewhere Else

One of the most popular options for backpackers and long-term travelers is a one-way rental. Instead of riding the same road twice, you pick up your bike in Ho Chi Minh City and drop it off in Da Nang or Hanoi when you reach the end of your journey. It's the ultimate way to see Vietnam north to south.

At Red Lantern Bikes, we offer one-way rentals to Da Nang and Hanoi. The process is simple: rent your bike in Saigon, ride at your own pace, and hand it back at the destination. Pricing for one-way rentals varies by bike and duration — contact us via WhatsApp for a quick quote.

How to Book Your Motorbike Rental in HCMC

Booking with Red Lantern Bikes takes two minutes. Browse our fleet above, choose your dates, and either pay a small deposit online to reserve your bike, or send us a message on WhatsApp. We confirm within minutes and there are no complicated forms or contracts.

We are located at 235B/A11/9 Nguyen Van Cu, District 1 — a short Grab ride from the tourist centre of Saigon. We are open every day and can deliver the bike to your hotel in District 1 for a small fee.

title: Ho Chi Minh City to Hanoi by Motorbike: The Complete Route Guide (2026)
metaTitle: Saigon to Hanoi by Motorbike 2026 – Full Route Guide | Red Lantern Bik
metaDescription: The complete Saigon to Hanoi motorbike route: 2,500–3,500km, 21–30 days, coast, mountains, national parks. Every stop explained with distances, tips, and which bike to rent.
html:
Riding a motorbike from Ho Chi Minh City to Hanoi is one of the greatest road trips on earth. Not just in Southeast Asia — on earth. More than 2,500 kilometres of everything Vietnam has to offer: steaming national parks, dramatic mountain passes, ancient imperial cities, turquoise coastline, misty highland plateaus and remote jungle roads that feel like you have the entire country to yourself.

This is not a trip you rush. The riders who get the most out of it take 21 to 30 days, cover 2,500 to 3,500km depending on their route, and come home completely changed. This guide follows our recommended itinerary — one that balances the best of the coast with the best of the mountains — and gives you everything you need to plan and ride it.

If you have more than 30 days, we have added a Northern Extension at the end covering Sa Pa, Ha Giang and Cao Bang — arguably the most spectacular riding in all of Southeast Asia.

The Route at a Glance

Total distance: 2,500–3,500km depending on diversions and side trips

Recommended duration: 21–30 days (core route) | 35–40 days (with northern extension)

Difficulty: Moderate to challenging — a mix of smooth coastal highways, winding mountain passes, and occasional rough highland roads

Best months: November to April for the south and centre; March to May or September to November for the north

The core stops in order: HCMC → Cat Tien National Park → Da Lat → Phan Rang → Nha Trang → Mang Den → Hoi An → Hue → Khe Sanh → Phong Nha National Park → Hoa Binh → Mai Chau → Pu Luong → Ninh Binh → Hanoi

Which Bike Should You Ride?

For a trip of this length and variety — coast, mountains, highland passes, and occasional rough roads — bike choice matters more than for a city rental. You need something with enough power for mountain passes, enough range between fuel stops in remote areas, and a service history you can trust.

Our top recommendation is the Kawasaki Versys X300. At 300cc it handles every pass on this route without struggling, the upright adventure riding position is comfortable across long days in the saddle, and the included top box carries everything you need for a month on the road. The Honda CB150X is a strong alternative for riders who want something lighter and more economical, and works perfectly for this route if you take your time.

Avoid the cheap Honda Win or semi-automatic bikes sold on the street. They may look like a bargain but a breakdown on the Ho Chi Minh Road, three hours from the nearest town, is not a bargain. Rent a properly maintained, fuel-injected bike from a reputable shop.

The Itinerary — Stop by Stop

Stop 1: Ho Chi Minh City (Days 1–2)

Distance from previous stop: Starting point

Recommended stay: 1–2 days

Spend a day or two in Saigon before you leave. Pick up your bike, get comfortable with it in city traffic, pack your bags, and eat well — the food in HCMC is some of the best in Vietnam. Visit Ben Thanh Market, walk along Bui Vien Street, and get an early night before Day 1 on the road.

Practical tip: load your top box the night before and do a short test ride through the city. If anything feels wrong with the bike, you want to find out now — not on a mountain pass two hundred kilometres from the shop.

Stop 2: Cat Tien National Park (Days 2–3)

Distance from HCMC: ~150km | 3–4 hours

Recommended stay: 1–2 nights

Your first destination is Cat Tien National Park, one of the largest and most biodiverse lowland rainforests in Vietnam. The ride north out of Saigon is straightforward — mostly flat, good road surfaces — and gives you a gentle introduction to riding in Vietnam before the terrain gets more dramatic.

Cat Tien is home to sun bears, crocodiles, over 350 bird species, and one of the last populations of Javan rhinoceros (now likely extinct here, but the forest remains extraordinary). Take a boat trip across the river to the park entrance, hire a guide for an evening wildlife walk, and sleep to the sound of the jungle. It is a world away from Saigon and the perfect way to start the journey.

Stop 3: Da Lat (Days 4–7)

Distance from Cat Tien: ~200km | 4–5 hours

Recommended stay: 2–3 nights

The climb from the lowlands up to Da Lat is one of the most dramatic in southern Vietnam. The temperature drops noticeably as you gain altitude and the landscape shifts from tropical forest to pine trees, strawberry farms, flower gardens, and misty valleys. At 1,500 metres, Da Lat feels like no other city in Vietnam.

The city itself is charming and walkable — French colonial architecture, a cable car, a crazy house you have to see to believe, and the best coffee in the country grown in the surrounding hills. The roads around Da Lat offer some excellent riding, particularly the descent towards the coast. Take at least two full days here.

Riding tip: the road from Cat Tien to Da Lat climbs sharply in the final 50km. Take it slowly, stay in a lower gear, and enjoy the views. The road is well-surfaced and not technically difficult.

Stop 4: Phan Rang (Days 8)

Distance from Da Lat: ~110km | 2.5–3 hours

The descent from Da Lat to the coast at Phan Rang is one of the best sections of road on the entire trip. You drop from 1,500 metres to sea level in about 50 kilometres, through switchbacks and hairpin turns with views over the coastal plains and the South China Sea. Take it slow, stop often, and take photos.

Phan Rang itself is not a major tourist destination, and that is part of its appeal. It sits in Vietnam's driest region — a semi-arid landscape of sand dunes, cactus, and ancient Cham towers that look completely unlike anywhere else in the country. The Po Klong Garai towers are 1,000 years old and absolutely worth a stop. Eat fresh seafood, sleep well, and get ready for Nha Trang.

Stop 5: Nha Trang (Days 8–10)

Distance from Phan Rang: ~100km | 2 hours

Recommended stay: 1–2 nights

Nha Trang is Vietnam's beach resort city — busy, commercial, and very popular with both domestic and international tourists. The beach is long and the water is clear. After a week on the road it is a good place to rest, do laundry, eat well, and swim.

Do not spend too long here. Nha Trang is enjoyable but it is the least authentic stop on this route. One beach day and a seafood dinner is enough for most riders. The real highlights of this trip lie further north.

Stop 6: Mang Den (Days 11–13)

Distance from Nha Trang: ~270km | 5–6 hours

Recommended stay: 2 nights

Mang Den is the hidden gem of this itinerary and the stop that most riders remember longest. Sitting at 1,200 metres in Kon Tum Province, it is a cool, misty highland plateau surrounded by ancient forests, waterfalls, and traditional Bahnar and Xedang minority villages. Barely touched by tourism, it feels like discovering a secret.

The road from Nha Trang to Mang Den climbs into the central highlands through increasingly remote terrain. The final stretch on Highway 24 from Kon Tum up to Mang Den is spectacular — forest-lined switchbacks, cool air, almost no traffic, and views over the Dak Bla River valley below.

Spend two nights here. Walk to the waterfalls, visit a minority village, eat at a local market stall, and watch the mist roll in over the pine forests at dusk. This is the real Vietnam.

Stop 7: Hoi An (Days 14–15)

Distance from Mang Den: ~200km | 4–5 hours

Recommended stay: 2 nights

The descent from the highlands to the coast brings you to Hoi An, the UNESCO-listed ancient trading port and one of the most beautiful towns in Southeast Asia. The old town is a maze of lantern-lit streets, centuries-old merchant houses, tailor shops, and riverside restaurants. It is touristy, yes — but deservedly so.

Give yourself two full nights here. Walk the old town at dawn before the crowds arrive, take a bicycle out to the rice paddies, eat Cao Lau noodles for every meal, and have a shirt made by one of the local tailors. Hoi An is the kind of place that makes you want to stay a week.

Riding note: park your motorbike outside the old town — vehicles are restricted in the historic centre. Most guesthouses have secure parking.

Stop 8: Hue (Days 16–17)

Distance from Hoi An: ~130km | 3 hours via Hai Van Pass

Recommended stay: 2 nights

The road from Hoi An to Hue crosses the Hai Van Pass — the most famous stretch of road in Vietnam. The pass climbs 500 metres above sea level along the spine of the Truong Son mountains, with the East Sea on one side and forested peaks on the other. On a clear day the views are extraordinary. Take your time.

Top Gear fans will recognise the Hai Van Pass from Series 12 — Jeremy Clarkson called it one of the greatest roads in the world. On a motorbike, it is even better than it looks on television.

Hue is Vietnam's former imperial capital and deserves serious time. The Citadel, the Royal Tombs, the Thien Mu Pagoda on the Perfume River — there is more history here than you can absorb in two days. The food is also exceptional: bun bo Hue is one of Vietnam's greatest dishes and you should eat it every morning for breakfast.

Stop 9: Khe Sanh (Day 18)

Distance from Hue: ~165km | 3.5–4 hours

Recommended stay: 1 night

The road west from Hue along Highway 9 takes you to Khe Sanh, the site of one of the most famous and brutal battles of the American War — the 77-day siege of 1968. The Khe Sanh Combat Base museum is sobering and important. Walking the red laterite soil of the old airstrip, surrounded by the same mountains that defined the battle, makes the history feel very immediate.

Beyond the history, the road to Khe Sanh is superb — the stretch through the mountains west of Hue is some of the best riding on the entire trip, with little traffic and dramatic scenery. The town itself is small and quiet. Sleep well; the next day's ride to Phong Nha is one of the best of the journey.

Stop 10: Phong Nha National Park (Days 19–21)

Distance from Khe Sanh: ~180km | 4 hours

Recommended stay: 2–3 nights

Phong Nha is the most spectacular natural attraction in Vietnam and arguably in all of Southeast Asia. The national park contains the world's largest cave — Son Doong — along with hundreds of other cave systems, the largest of which were only discovered in the 1990s and are still being mapped. The rivers run underground through limestone mountains and emerge as turquoise pools in jungle valleys.

You do not need to do the $3,000 Son Doong expedition to have an unforgettable experience here. Paradise Cave is one of the most dramatic cave systems you will ever walk through. Phong Nha Cave by boat on the underground river is eerie and beautiful. The Dark Cave involves zip lines, kayaking, and mud swimming in a cave — an extraordinary afternoon.

The town of Phong Nha village is small, friendly, and full of good guesthouses and restaurants set up specifically for riders doing the north-south route. Stay at least two nights. Ride the roads around the park — the Ho Chi Minh Road north of Phong Nha is empty, forested, and one of the best stretches of riding in Vietnam.

Stop 11: Hoa Binh (Days 22–23)

Distance from Phong Nha: ~350km | 6–7 hours

Recommended stay: 1 night

The long ride north from Phong Nha to Hoa Binh takes you along the Ho Chi Minh Road through Nghe An and Ha Tinh provinces — the heartland of north-central Vietnam. This is a long day in the saddle but the road is beautiful: winding through forested hills with almost no tourist traffic.

Hoa Binh is a transit stop rather than a destination. The Hoa Binh reservoir and dam are impressive at scale, and the surrounding hills are home to Muong and Dao minority communities. Stay one night and push on towards Mai Chau in the morning.

Stop 12: Mai Chau (Day 23)

Distance from Hoa Binh: ~60km | 1.5 hours

Recommended stay: 1–2 nights

Mai Chau Valley is everything you imagine when you picture rural northern Vietnam: a flat, emerald-green valley floor of rice paddies surrounded on all sides by karst limestone peaks, with White Thai stilt houses dotting the landscape. It is genuinely beautiful and not yet overrun by tourism.

The valley itself is best explored by bicycle rather than motorbike — hire one from your guesthouse and pedal between villages in the late afternoon light. Eat dinner in a traditional stilt house, sleep on a mattress on the communal floor, and wake up to mist rolling off the mountains at dawn. One of the most peaceful nights on the entire trip.

Stop 13: Pu Luong Nature Reserve (Days 24–25)

Distance from Mai Chau: ~60km | 1.5–2 hours

Recommended stay: 1–2 nights

Pu Luong is one of the most beautiful and least-visited natural areas in northern Vietnam. The reserve protects a long valley of terraced rice fields, traditional Thai villages, wooden watermills, and forested limestone ridges. The landscape in the late afternoon — golden rice terraces stacked up the hillsides, smoke rising from the stilt houses — looks like a painting.

The road through Pu Luong is narrow and winding, which makes it perfect for motorbike exploration. Ride slowly, stop constantly, and talk to the farmers working the terraces. There are excellent homestay guesthouses throughout the valley — simple, clean, and run by local families who cook extraordinary traditional meals.

Stop 14: Ninh Binh — Tam Coc (Days 26–27)

Distance from Pu Luong: ~100km | 2.5–3 hours

Recommended stay: 1–2 nights

The approach to Ninh Binh through the limestone karst landscape of Tam Coc is one of the most visually dramatic moments of the entire trip. Jagged limestone peaks rise directly from flat rice paddies, their reflections perfectly mirrored in the flooded fields. It looks unreal.

Take a rowing boat through the Tam Coc caves — three river caves carved through limestone mountains, rowed by local women who steer with their feet so their hands are free to wave at tourists. Visit Trang An, the UNESCO-listed landscape of interconnected waterways and grottos. Climb the 500 steps to Hang Mua viewpoint at sunset for the best panorama in the region.

Ninh Binh is the last great stop before Hanoi. Take your time and enjoy it.

Stop 15: Hanoi (Days 28–30)

Distance from Ninh Binh: ~100km | 2 hours

Recommended stay: 2–3 days

The final ride into Hanoi is the end of one of the great journeys in the world. You left Ho Chi Minh City three to four weeks ago and you have crossed the entire length of Vietnam — from the tropics to the north, through jungles, coastlines, mountain passes, highland plateaus, ancient cities, and landscapes that look like nowhere else on earth.

Hanoi is a worthy end point. The Old Quarter is a genuine labyrinth of 1,000-year-old streets, each historically dedicated to a single trade. Hoan Kiem Lake in the morning mist, a bowl of pho at a street stall before dawn, the Temple of Literature, the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum, and the best bia hoi (fresh draft beer, served from plastic stools on the pavement for 20 cents a glass) in the world.

Drop your bike at our designated Hanoi partner drop-off point, get a bus or taxi to the airport or train station, and start planning the next trip.

Northern Extension: For Riders with 30+ Days

If you have more time, do not fly home from Hanoi. The mountains of northwest and northeast Vietnam — Sa Pa, Ha Giang, and Cao Bang — are not just an extension of this trip. They are arguably the best riding in all of Southeast Asia, and many experienced riders say they are more spectacular than anything on the main route south.

Add 7–12 days and a further 1,000–1,500km. The roads are more challenging — narrower, steeper, and occasionally unpaved — but the scenery and the experience are on a completely different level.

Sa Pa (Days 31–33)

Distance from Hanoi: ~350km | 6–7 hours | or overnight train to Lao Cai + 30 min ride

Recommended stay: 2–3 nights

Sa Pa sits at 1,500 metres in the Hoang Lien Son mountains on the border with China, and on a clear day you can see Fansipan — at 3,143 metres, the highest peak in Indochina — rising above the town. The terraced rice fields of the Muong Hoa Valley below Sa Pa, cultivated for centuries by the H'Mong and Red Dao minority peoples, are some of the most photographed landscapes in Vietnam.

The ride from Hanoi to Sa Pa follows Highway 32 northwest through Mu Cang Chai — one of the finest stretches of mountain road in the country, particularly in late September and October when the rice terraces turn gold at harvest time. The road climbs through tropical forest, above the cloud line, and descends through valley after valley of terraced fields.

From Sa Pa, ride the O Quy Ho Pass — the highest road pass in Vietnam at 2,073 metres — on a clear morning. The views on the descent towards Lai Chau are extraordinary.

Ha Giang (Days 34–37)

Distance from Sa Pa: ~300km | 6–7 hours

Recommended stay: 3–4 nights

Ha Giang is the most remote province in Vietnam and home to the most spectacular motorcycle road in the country: the Dong Van Karst Plateau Geopark. The Ma Pi Leng Pass, carved into near-vertical cliffs above the Nho Que River, is regularly cited by experienced riders as one of the greatest roads in the world. The canyon below is 700 metres deep. The road is paved, single-lane, and extraordinary.

The Ha Giang Loop — typically 3–4 days of riding through Quan Ba, Yen Minh, Dong Van, and Meo Vac — takes you through landscapes that look Martian: bare limestone peaks, isolated H'Mong villages clinging to cliffsides, buckwheat fields in shades of pink and white, and a canyon that makes the rest of Vietnam look flat.

Ha Giang receives far fewer tourists than Sa Pa or Hoi An. The roads are quiet, the scenery is relentless, and the sense of remoteness is real. This is the kind of riding that people plan their entire Vietnam trip around.

Cao Bang (Days 38–40)

Distance from Ha Giang: ~200km | 5–6 hours on mountain roads

Recommended stay: 2 nights

Cao Bang, in the far northeast of Vietnam on the Chinese border, is the final and least-visited stop of the northern extension. The highlight is Ban Gioc Waterfall — at 300 metres wide, the largest waterfall in Southeast Asia and one of the most powerful in the world. The falls straddle the border between Vietnam and China; you can rent a bamboo raft to get close to the base.

The road from Ha Giang to Cao Bang crosses the Mã Phục Pass and winds through limestone karst country that feels genuinely remote. You may ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle. The area around Cao Bang was the birthplace of the Vietnamese revolution — the Pac Bo cave where Ho Chi Minh lived in hiding in 1941 is a short ride from town.

From Cao Bang, ride south back towards Hanoi through Lang Son — a long but straightforward day on good roads. Return your bike, celebrate with a cold Hanoi beer, and start counting the days until you can come back.

Essential Practical Tips

How to plan your daily distances

150–200km per day is a comfortable average that leaves time for stops, photography, and exploring. Resist the urge to ride 350km days to 'make time' — the roads you skip are usually the best ones. The riders who regret this trip are the ones who went too fast.

Fuel

Petrol stations are plentiful on the coast and main highways. In the highlands and on the Ho Chi Minh Road, gaps between stations can be 80–100km. 

Weather

Vietnam's weather is regional and counterintuitive. When the south and centre are dry (November–April), the north can be cold and foggy. The central coast (Hoi An to Hue) has its own rainy season in October–December. The best months for the full north-south route are February to April. Check regional forecasts, not national ones.

Accommodation

Do not book too far in advance. Guesthouses are plentiful at every stop on this itinerary. Book the night before using Booking.com or Agoda, or just roll in and look. The flexibility to stay an extra day somewhere wonderful is one of the great luxuries of this style of travel.

Budget

Budget approximately $35–55 per day covering accommodation ($10–20), food ($8–15), fuel ($2-5), and incidentals. The motorbike rental is a separate cost. Total trip cost excluding flights: approximately $800–1,500 depending on your pace and comfort level.

Road safety

• Ride in the morning. Start by 7am, stop by 2pm when fatigue and heat peak

• Wear a full-face helmet — Red Lantern Bikes provides one with every rental

• Stay on the left on highways; Vietnamese roads follow left-hand traffic

• Watch for cattle, dogs, and children on rural roads — especially at dawn

• Save our WhatsApp number before you leave — we provide roadside support anywhere in Vietnam

• Get travel insurance that explicitly covers motorcycle riding — check your policy carefully

Ready to Start?

Red Lantern Bikes offers one-way rental from Ho Chi Minh City — pick up your bike at our shop in District 1 and drop it off in Hanoi when you arrive. We can advise on bike choice, prepare your bike for a long-distance trip, and are on WhatsApp if anything goes wrong along the way.

Browse our fleet, choose your dates, and reserve with a $50 deposit. The road is waiting.

title: Best Motorbikes to Rent in Vietnam (2026)
metaTitle: Best Motorbikes to Rent in Vietnam 2026 – Beginner Guide | Red Lantern
metaDescription: Not sure which motorbike to rent in Vietnam? This 2026 guide compares the best options for beginners and experienced riders — by riding style, budget, and route.
html:
One of the first questions every traveler asks us is: which bike should I rent? It's a fair question. Vietnam has dozens of options across wildly different price ranges and riding styles. Choosing the wrong bike can make your trip stressful. Choosing the right one makes it unforgettable.

This guide breaks down the best motorbikes available in Vietnam by rider experience and intended route, so you can make the right call before you arrive.

For Absolute Beginners: Honda Wave Alpha 110cc

Rental price: From $7/day

Best for: Zero riding experience, super reliable, easy to fix, the most fun scooter

The Honda Wave is the backbone of Vietnamese transport. Walk through any street in Saigon and you'll see hundreds of them. Semi-automatic (with gears but super easy to learn), light enough to maneuver through traffic, fuel-efficient, and virtually impossible to break. For a first-time rider exploring Ho Chi Minh City or doing the whole country, this is the bike.

The 110cc engine won't win any races, but you don't need speed in Vietnam, you need reliability and maneuverability. The Wave gives you both.

For Riders who wants on and off-road: Honda XR150

Rental price: From $12/day

Best for: City + countryside, light off-road, multi-day trips

The Honda XR150 is our most popular rental for a reason. It sits in the sweet spot between easy handling and genuine capability. The manual transmission is approachable for riders who have some experience but have not ridden much recently, and the 150cc engine has enough power for coastal highways and any mountain roads.

It handles light dirt roads and gravel tracks well, making it ideal if your route takes you off the main highways and through rural Vietnam. Comfortable enough for 200km days, easy enough for a morning spent navigating Saigon traffic.

For Experienced Riders: Honda CB150X

Rental price: From $22/day

Best for: Coastal touring, multi-week trips, adventure riding

The Honda CB150X is a step up in comfort and style. The upright adventure riding position is ergonomically designed for longer days in the saddle, and the 150cc fuel-injected engine delivers smooth, consistent power across Vietnam's range of road surfaces.

If you're planning two weeks or more on the road and want a bike that feels planted on the coastal highways and confident on the mountain passes of central Vietnam, the CB150X is worth the extra $10/day.

For Long-Distance Touring: Kawasaki Versys X300

Rental price: From $35/day

Best for: Full Saigon–Hanoi route, mountain passes, experienced riders

The Kawasaki Versys X300 is in a different league from the bikes above. A genuine adventure tourer with 300cc of power, ABS braking, and a large top box included — it's the bike you want for the serious north-south Vietnam ride.

The Versys handles the Hai Van Pass above Da Nang and the mountain climbs through the central highlands with genuine composure. It's comfortable over 300km days and carries enough luggage for two weeks away from home. We recommend this bike for riders who have at least a year of regular riding experience.

Quick Comparison Table

• • Honda Wave 110cc | $7/day | Beginner | City & short trips | Semi-auto

• • Honda XR150 | $12/day | Intermediate | Full Vietnam and Off-road | Manual

• • Honda CB150X | $22/day | Experienced | Coastal touring | Manual

• • Kawasaki Versys X300 | $35/day | Experienced | Full Vietnam | Manual + ABS

Still Not Sure? Ask Us.

If you're still not sure which bike is right for your trip, just WhatsApp us. Tell us your experience level, your planned route, and your budget — and we'll recommend the best option from our fleet. We've helped hundreds of riders plan their Vietnam adventure and we're happy to help you do the same.

Browse our full fleet and available dates above, or message us directly to reserve your bike with a small deposit. We're based in District 1, Ho Chi Minh City, and open every day.
